title: Magnetic Circuits — Fundamentals
subtitle: This week introduces the magnetic equivalent of an electric circuit. Every concept here has a direct electrical analogue — once you see the pattern, the whole topic unlocks. The key insight: flux follows magnetic paths the same way current follows wires.
learningOutcome: This week introduces the magnetic equivalent of an electric circuit. Every concept here has a direct electrical analogue — once you see the pattern, the whole topic unlocks. The key insight: flux follows magnetic paths the same way current follows wires.

content.text: Magnetism shows up in every electrical machine — motors, generators, transformers. You cannot escape it. So let's nail it properly.

Around every magnet (and around every wire carrying current), there exists a magnetic field — an invisible region where magnetic forces act. We visualise this field using magnetic flux lines (symbol: φ, pronounced "phi"). Think of flux lines as the "flow paths" of magnetism.

Four rules about flux lines — know these cold: ① They always form closed loops — they never start or end anywhere. ② They travel from North to South outside the magnet, and South to North inside. ③ They never cross each other. ④ They take the shortest, highest-permeability path available.
The SI unit of magnetic flux is the Weber (Wb).

Think of it like this Magnetic flux lines are like water flowing in a closed pipe loop — the water always flows in a loop, never disappearing at one end. And just like water prefers wider pipes (less resistance), flux prefers materials with high permeability (less reluctance).

Examinable definition:
"Unlike electric field lines, magnetic flux lines always form closed loops — they have no beginning or end."

content.text: Flux (φ) tells you the total amount of magnetism passing through a surface. But flux density (B) tells you how concentrated that flux is — how many Webers pass through each square metre. This is the more useful engineering quantity.
Squash the same flux into a smaller area → flux density goes up. Spread it over a bigger area → flux density goes down. Same total, different concentration.
Magnetic flux density
B = magnetic flux density (T, where 1 T = 1 Wb/m²) φ = total magnetic flux (Weber, Wb) A = cross-sectional area of the magnetic path (m²) Rearranged: φ = B × A

Think of it like this Shine a torch at a wall. Total light output (lumens) = flux φ. Move the torch closer — same light, smaller circle on the wall, brighter spot. That brightness per unit area is flux density B. Same φ, smaller A → higher B.

Common mistake — Students confuse φ (total flux, in Wb) with B (flux density, in T). They are not the same thing. B = φ/A. If a question gives flux and area → divide to find B. If it gives B and area → multiply to find φ. Plugging the wrong quantity into the wrong formula is one of the most common ways to lose marks on this topic.

topics.title: MMF, Magnetising Force H & Permeability μ

subtopics.title: MMF, Magnetising Force H & Permeability μ

content.text: Magnetomotive Force (MMF) is what drives flux through a magnetic circuit — exactly like EMF drives current through an electric circuit. For a coil of N turns carrying current I: MMF (F) = NI, measured in Ampere-turns (A·t).

Magnetising Force H is the MMF per unit length of the magnetic path. It tells you how much "magnetic pressure" is applied per metre of the path. The same MMF applied to a short path gives a higher H than if applied to a long path.

Permeability (μ) is the magnetic equivalent of conductivity — it measures how easily a material allows flux through it. μ = μ₀ × μᵣ, where μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m is the permeability of free space and μᵣ is the relative permeability of the material (dimensionless). For air: μᵣ = 1. For silicon steel: μᵣ can reach 1000–10000.
MMF, H, and permeability

N = number of turns · I = current (A) · L = mean path length (m) μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m (permeability of free space) μᵣ = relative permeability — dimensionless, material-specific High μᵣ → easy to magnetise (silicon steel, soft iron)

topics.title: Reluctance & Ohm's Law for Magnetic Circuits

subtopics.title: Reluctance & Ohm's Law for Magnetic Circuits

content.text: Reluctance (ℛ) is the opposition a magnetic path offers to flux — the magnetic equivalent of resistance. A long, thin path through a low-permeability material has high reluctance. A short, wide path through a high-permeability material has low reluctance.

The magnetic Ohm's Law completes the analogy: just like V = IR drives current through resistance, MMF = φ × ℛ drives flux through reluctance. This is the single most important relationship in magnetic circuit analysis.
Reluctance & Magnetic Ohm's Law
L = mean path length (m) · A = cross-sectional area (m²) μ₀μᵣ = absolute permeability of the material (H/m) Compare: V ↔ F(MMF) · I ↔ φ(flux) · R ↔ ℛ(reluctance)

The electric–magnetic analogy (frequent exam question):
EMF (V) ↔ MMF (NI, A·t) Current (I, A) ↔ Flux (φ, Wb) Resistance (R, Ω) ↔ Reluctance (ℛ, A·t/Wb) Conductivity (σ) ↔ Permeability (μ) Ohm's Law: V = IR ↔ F = φℛ

Common mistake — The reluctance formula uses absolute permeability μ₀μᵣ — not just μᵣ alone. Writing ℛ = L/(μᵣA) instead of ℛ = L/(μ₀μᵣA) gives an answer that's 4π×10⁷ times too large. Always include μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m in the denominator.
